newsitem.title: USA: U.S. firefighters attack Montana blaze from air.
newsitem.headline: U.S. firefighters attack Montana blaze from air.

text.p: Firefighters launched an air attack on Friday on a fast-growing Montana wildfire that has consumed 11,000 acres (4,450 hectares) of forest and destroyed 28 summer homes, officials said.

Fire officials planned to use five helicopters and several planes to drop water and fire retardant on the Shepard Mountain fire in the Custer National Forest in southern Montana, national forest spokeswoman Sherry Milburn said.
Strong winds and swirling smoke prevented use of aircraft on Thursday, but the wind died down and temperatures cooled on Friday, aiding firefighters, Milburn said.

The lightning-caused fire had burned slowly for 10 days before it suddenly blew up on Wednesday, growing from 650 acres (260 hectares) to 8,000 acres (3,200 hectares) by Thursday and 11,000 acres (4,450 hectares) by Friday.
The fire, burning about 20 miles (32 kms) west of the town of Red Lodge, has destroyed 28 summer cabins and several other buildings were feared lost, Milburn said.
About 65 people had to be evacuated from the area earlier this week, officials said. Two firefighters have been injured, including one who suffered second-degree burns.
The Montana fire was the most troublesome of the blazes still burning in the Western United States, which has had its worst wildfire season in 30 years.

The Boise, Idaho-based National Interagency Fire Centre said more than 10,150 firefighters were battling 10 major fires burning on 181,000 acres (73,250 hectares) in Idaho, Montana, Oregon and Wyoming on Friday. Last week, 52 fires were burning across the West, stretching resources to the limit, but cooler weather and rain in places has helped firefighters bring many under control.

Firefighters were using air tankers and helicopters to battle a stubborn fire in the Big Horn National Forest in Wyoming. The fire more than doubled in size to 2,200 acres (890 hectares) on Thursday but has grown very little since.
